text: Ugolino Lifts His Mouth from His Enemy's Skull: Why Must a Victim's Truth Also Leave the Children a Place of Their Own?
Dante first sees two heads frozen in the same hole in the ice.
The soul above is biting into the skull of the soul below from behind.
His teeth sink into the place where the brain meets the nape, like a hungry person tearing at bread.
Dante asks:
Why do you hate him so?
If your accusation is just, I can make his crime known when I return to the world of the living.
The gnawing figure raises his mouth.
He wipes away the blood with the hair he has been tearing at.
Then he says:
You ask me to awaken a grief that crushes my heart merely to think of it, before I even speak.
But if my words can bear the fruit of infamy, making the traitor I gnaw more shameful in the living world, then I am willing to speak and weep together.
He gives his name:
Count Ugolino.
The man he bites is Archbishop Ruggieri.
From the first sentence, his telling has two purposes.
Ugolino wants to tell how he and his young relatives were shut in a tower, denied food, and starved to death.
This is a real atrocity.
He also explicitly wants this truth to go on punishing his enemy's reputation.
Both things can be true at once.
A narrative does not automatically become a lie because it serves revenge.
Equally, the truth of its facts does not place every use of the narrative beyond question.
This is the hardest part of the story to handle.

If noticing the desire for revenge makes us doubt whether what happened in the starvation tower deserves condemnation, we require a victim first to be free of anger and any wish for retaliation before deserving belief.
But if the reality of the atrocity makes us think we must never question how Ugolino arranges all the people in his account, the other dead remain confined to his purposes.
Ugolino says they were imprisoned in a narrow tower.
Through a small window, they saw the moon many times.
Then he had a terrible dream.
In it, hunters and hounds pursued a wolf and its young, finally tearing into their bodies.
When he woke, he heard the young people weeping in their sleep and asking for bread.
Then the door below was nailed shut.
Ugolino silently looked at his young relatives.
He did not weep.
Inside, he was hardened like stone.
They wept.
Asked their father what was wrong.
He still said nothing.
Through the next day and the day after, until faint daylight entered the tower and he saw his own likeness in the children's faces.
Pain made him bite his hands.
Thinking that he wanted to eat from hunger, the young people said:
Father, if you eat our bodies, we will suffer a little less.
You gave us this flesh.
Now you may take it back.
These words come to us only through Ugolino's account.
The children have no independent narration in the poem.
Readers do not know how each understood their father, imprisonment, or death.
How much fear, comfort, despair, or self-sacrifice lay in their words.
We can hear only the version their father remembers.
This does not mean that his account must be untrustworthy.
The preservation of loved ones' last words amid extreme trauma is itself an important way history enters the world.
But “retold by the father” remains a fact.
When the whole story is organized by someone who survived until the end, the other dead can easily appear only in ways that intensify the narrator's pain and accusation.
They are his children.
They are also themselves.
The historical relationships in the poem do not entirely match what modern readers imagine on hearing “children.”
Historical annotations commonly identify those imprisoned with Ugolino as two sons and two grandsons.
The poem's paternal language also gathers them together as his descendants and loved ones.
An essay for general readers need not use genealogy to correct mourning.
But it must avoid treating the four young people as nothing but a collective whole.
They were imprisoned because of adults' political conflicts.
Whatever Ugolino's political betrayals, alliances, or responsibilities in power, kinship alone should not have condemned them to death by starvation.
After Ugolino's account, Dante also condemns Pisa directly:
Even if the count was infamous for betraying castles, the young people should not have been punished with him.
This judgment is stronger than Ugolino's personal defense.
The poem itself confirms that children cannot serve as substitute payment for their fathers' guilt.
The young people begin to die one by one.
On the fourth day, Gaddo falls at his father's feet and asks:
Father, why do you not help me?
Then he dies.
Between the fifth and sixth days, the others fall in turn.
Ugolino can no longer see and can only grope for their bodies in the darkness.
After their deaths, he calls out for two more days.
His final sentence says:
Hunger was stronger than grief.
This sentence has provoked debate for centuries.
Some understand it simply to mean that hunger finally killed Ugolino.
Others find in it a terrible suggestion that he ate the corpses.
The poem gives no explanation sufficient to settle the question.
So “the father ate the children in the end” cannot be stated as fact.
This uncertainty is not a gap to be smoothed over for the sake of a fluent story.
It is part of the text itself.
The ambiguous final sentence can also steal the children's place.
If reading focuses entirely on “did he eat human flesh or not,” the imprisonment, fear, and deaths of four young people once again become material for making the count a figure of horror.
The question of cannibalism certainly has literary force.
But the atrocity the poem has already established does not depend on that unresolved question.
The door was sealed.
Food stopped coming.
The young people died one by one.
Their father groped for their bodies in the dark.
This is already enough.
What is uncertain should remain uncertain.
The harm that is certain should remain certain too.
When Ugolino finishes speaking, he does not stop gnawing.
He seizes Ruggieri's skull with his teeth again.
The telling has not transformed revenge into forgiveness.
Nor has it established an earthly court.
Through his enemy's body, he continues his own punishment and retaliation.
Ruggieri is both the perpetrator and the person being gnawed at this moment.
Ugolino is both a victim of the starvation tower and a soul being punished in Hell's region of traitors.
Different positions a person occupies overlap within the same picture.
Acknowledging the terrible harm he suffered does not require restoring his whole life and present actions to blamelessness.
Equally, his own guilt cannot justify Ruggieri and Pisa starving the young people to death.
We easily want to make complicated relationships clean.
Either Ugolino is an innocent father and Ruggieri is pure evil.
Or Ugolino was a traitor, so what happened belongs to the consequences of politics.
Dante refuses both simplifications.
He places Ugolino in the frozen lake of traitors, without declaring his entire political life innocent.
And he curses Pisa's cruelty toward the young in the strongest language.
A person may be responsible for certain things and, in another matter, suffer an atrocity that should never have been inflicted on them.
Responsibility is not an overall score.
Guilt in one matter does not permit others to do anything they like to that person and their family.
Nor does being a victim in one matter justify everything that person does afterward.
Why is Ugolino willing to speak?
To make Ruggieri infamous among the living.
This purpose is entirely understandable.
When a perpetrator conceals harm through power, status, or historical narrative, a victim's telling of the facts will naturally change reputations.
Damage to reputation is not a side effect outside the story.
It may be the only way to bring responsibility into public memory.
Requiring a victim to give only a “neutral statement,” without wishing for condemnation of the perpetrator, amounts to asking him to forgo the most important public consequence of speaking.
This essay therefore cannot lightly dismiss “bringing shame on the enemy” as an impure motive.
The question is not why he wants Ruggieri disgraced.
It is this:
Within this legitimate accusation, do the other dead still have a place as more than evidence?
The young people's words make Ugolino a father in the deepest agony.
They are willing to let their father take back the bodies he gave them.
This greatly heightens Ruggieri's cruelty and the count's tragedy alike.
But if we understand them only through their father's suffering, they still have not left his story.
They were imprisoned because of adults' political conflicts.
After death, they become the most powerful part of the proof that one adult was victimized and another was evil.
This does not mean that Ugolino deliberately claims them for himself.
The poem can make the dead appear only through a speaker.
But after listening, readers can preserve an additional limit:
These young people are not merely “Ugolino's children.”
Nor do their deaths mean only that “their father suffered the cruelest thing imaginable.”
Each lost a life of their own.
Leaving the children a place of their own does not mean inventing a modern speech for them.
We do not know how they would assess their father's political actions.
Whether they were truly willing to feed him with their bodies.
Or what each wanted to say at the end.
Truly respecting the text does not mean filling the silence.
It means acknowledging:
Their father cannot determine their entire meaning for them.
Neither can the poet.
Nor can readers today.
Their lack of independent speech is precisely why we should speak for them less, not give ourselves greater freedom to put words in their mouths.
At least this is certain: adults' guilt, revenge, and reputations cannot make their deaths nothing more than usable material.
Is Ugolino's accusation truth, or narrative?
The two are not opposites.
For any truth to enter the public world, someone must organize it into a narrative.
Choose where to begin.
Which details to preserve.
What to call the people involved.
When to stop.
From the dream, the nailing of the door, hunger, the children's offer of themselves, and the deaths one by one, Ugolino builds a path that the listener cannot easily escape.
This path may run very close to the facts.
It also explicitly serves his revenge.
Examining how a narrative works does not mean that its facts can be ignored.
It merely acknowledges that facts and the purposes of telling can exist together.
Dante as listener initially sets a condition:
If your accusation is justified, I will spread it among the living for you.
This makes the poet's writing itself part of an exchange.
Ugolino tells of the hidden deaths.
Dante lets Ruggieri's infamy leave Hell and reenter the human world.
That we still know the name today shows that the exchange has been completed.
But spreading the perpetrator's infamy also spreads the details of the victims' torment.
The children's hunger, cries, and deaths become part of literary memory.
This may be the only way to resist forgetting.
For that very reason, it requires greater care from narrators and readers:
Do not let remembering an atrocity become yet another way merely to consume the suffering of the dead.
Ugolino keeps gnawing Ruggieri.
This is not a justice we must imitate.
Nor is it a psychological problem we can lightly condemn as “not letting go.”
The structure of eternal punishment in the Inferno freezes guilt and retaliation in the same action.
Ugolino cannot leave his enemy.
Ruggieri cannot leave the suffering he caused either.
They are bound forever in a relationship that defines each through the other.
The image reminds us:
Revenge can stop a perpetrator from escaping responsibility.
It may also leave the victim's own eternal identity as nothing more than someone who continues to harm the perpetrator.
If true earthly justice is possible, it should preserve responsibility without keeping every life forever at the moment when the harm occurred.
But this cannot become an appeal for Ugolino to make peace.
Persuading him to forgive Ruggieri is not this essay's task.
Still less can “revenge hurts you too” be used to minimize what happened in the starvation tower.
First, this must be made clear:
Imprisoning young people until they starve to death is an atrocity.
Whatever the count's political guilt, they should not have been treated this way.
Only once that judgment stands firm is there room to see:
How Ugolino tells his own story through their deaths.
How real his anger is.
How powerful his narrative is.
And how it still cannot contain all four dead within the two positions of “my pain” and “his infamy.”
A victim has the right to speak their own truth.
And to want the perpetrator remembered, held responsible, and stripped of a good reputation they should not retain.
Asking a narrative to leave room for other victims does not restrict the first victim's speech.
It prevents the same atrocity from becoming only the story of the person best able to tell it.
Ugolino can speak.
The young people cannot.
Precisely for that reason, the listener needs to do two things at once:
Let his accusation reach the living world in full.
And refuse to let the children exist forever only as its most shocking passage.
He lifts his mouth from his enemy's skull, speaks, and weeps.
When he finishes, he lowers his head and gnaws again.
This makes any clean conclusion impossible.
Truth and revenge share one mouth.
Paternal love and political guilt inhabit one person.
The voices of innocent young people reach us only through a father who is still being punished.
Perhaps reading this story seriously does not begin by deciding whether Ugolino is a good man or a bad one.
It begins by preserving together facts that cannot cancel one another out:
Ruggieri's atrocity must be remembered.
Ugolino's complex responsibilities cannot disappear because of it.
Still less should the children be jointly possessed by adults' guilt and narratives merely because they were imprisoned with their father.
Let the truth be spoken.
Let the perpetrator be unable to escape his name.
And let the dead young people belong to more than their father's revenge.

*Textual basis: Dante, Divine Comedy, the end of Inferno Canto 32 and Canto 33. At the end of Canto 32, Ugolino gnaws Ruggieri's skull from behind, and Dante offers to spread his accusation among the living if it is justified (Inf. 32.124–139). At the opening of Canto 33, Ugolino raises his mouth, wipes it with his enemy's hair, and explicitly says that if his account can bear the fruit of infamy for the traitor he gnaws, he is willing to weep and speak together (Inf. 33.1–12). He recounts the dream, the tower door being nailed shut, the cutting off of food, his young relatives' mistaken belief that he is biting his hands from hunger and their offer to let their father take back their bodies, their deaths one by one, and his groping and calling out in the darkness (approximately 33.13–75). The final sentence, “Hunger was stronger than grief,” has long been read both as hunger finally killing him and as a suggestion of eating the corpses. This essay does not present the latter as established fact. Dante then condemns Pisa: even if Ugolino is infamous for betraying castles, the young people should not have suffered this punishment (approximately 33.79–90). This essay first explicitly acknowledges the atrocity of imprisoning and starving the young to death, then distinguishes actual victimization, the purpose of telling, and the place the other dead must retain beyond serving as evidence for their father's accusation.*
